Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We present mid-infrared (10.4 \micron, 11.7 \micron, and 18.3 \micron) imaging intended to locate and characterize the suspected protostellar components within the Bok globule CB54. We detect and confirm the protostellar status for the near-infrared source CB54YC1-II. The mid-infrared luminosity for CB54YC1-II was found to be $L_{midir} \approx 8 L_\sun$, and we estimate a central source mass of $M_* \approx 0.8 M_\sun$ (for a mass accretion rate of ${\dot M}=10^{-6} M_\sun yr^{-1}$). CB54 harbors another near-infrared source (CB54YC1-I), which was not detected by our observations. The non-detection is consistent with CB54YC1-I being a highly extinguished embedded young A or B star or a background G or F giant. An alternative explanation for CB54YC1-I is that the source is an embedded protostar viewed at an extremely high inclination angle, and the near-infrared detections are not of the central protostar, but of light scattered by the accretion disk into our line of sight. In addition, we have discovered three new mid-infrared sources, which are spatially coincident with the previously known dense core in CB54. The source temperatures ($\sim100$K) and association of the mid-infrared sources with the dense core suggests that these mid-infrared objects may be embedded class 0 protostars.

outputs.L1: We present mid-infrared imaging at 10.4, 11.7, and 18.3 \micron aimed at locating and characterizing the suspected protostellar components within the Bok globule CB54. We detect the near-infrared source CB54YC1-II and confirm its protostellar nature. Its mid-infrared luminosity is estimated to be $L_{midir} \approx 8 L_\sun$, and we infer a central source mass of $M_* \approx 0.8 M_\sun$, assuming a mass accretion rate of ${\dot M}=10^{-6} M_\sun yr^{-1}$. CB54 also harbors another near-infrared source, CB54YC1-I, which was not detected in our observations. This non-detection is consistent with CB54YC1-I being either a highly extinguished, embedded young A or B star or a background G or F giant. Alternatively, CB54YC1-I may be an embedded protostar viewed at an extremely high inclination angle, such that the near-infrared detections trace not the central protostar itself, but rather light scattered into our line of sight by the accretion disk. In addition, we have discovered three new mid-infrared sources spatially coincident with the previously known dense core in CB54. Their temperatures ($\sim100$ K) and association with the dense core suggest that these objects may be embedded Class 0 protostars.
outputs.L2:
We report mid-infrared observations of the Bok globule CB54 at 10.4, 11.7, and 18.3 \micron, obtained to identify and investigate its proposed protostellar members. Our detection of the near-infrared object CB54YC1-II confirms that it is a protostar. We derive a mid-infrared luminosity of \(L_{\mathrm{midir}} \approx 8\,L_\sun\) and, assuming an accretion rate of \(\dot{M}=10^{-6}\,M_\sun\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}\), estimate the central object’s mass to be \(M_* \approx 0.8\,M_\sun\).

A second near-infrared source in CB54, CB54YC1-I, was absent from our mid-infrared detections. This result is compatible with either a deeply obscured, embedded young A- or B-type star or a background F- or G-type giant. Another possibility is that CB54YC1-I is an embedded protostar observed at an almost edge-on inclination. Under this interpretation, the near-infrared emission does not arise directly from the central protostar but instead consists of light redirected into our line of sight by scattering from the accretion disk.

We also identify three previously unknown mid-infrared objects whose positions coincide with the known dense core in CB54. Their temperatures of approximately \(100\) K, together with their association with the dense core, indicate that they may be embedded Class 0 protostars.
outputs.L3:
Mid-infrared imaging at wavelengths of 10.4, 11.7, and 18.3 microns was used to identify and characterize suspected protostellar components within the Bok globule CB54. These observations confirmed that CB54YC1-II is a protostar, with an estimated mid-infrared luminosity of approximately eight times that of the Sun and a mass of about 0.8 solar masses.

In contrast, CB54YC1-I was not detected at these wavelengths. This non-detection is consistent with several possible interpretations: the source may be a highly obscured young A- or B-type star, a background G- or F-type giant, or an embedded protostar viewed nearly edge-on and detected primarily through scattered light.

The observations also revealed three previously unknown mid-infrared sources located within the region of CB54’s known dense core. Their inferred temperatures are close to 100 K, suggesting that they may be deeply embedded Class 0 protostars. Together, these findings indicate that CB54 contains multiple young stellar objects at different stages of early evolution.
outputs.L4:
Bok globules are compact, isolated molecular clouds that often contain some of the youngest forming stars. To investigate the star-forming activity within the Bok globule CB54, mid-infrared images were obtained at 10.4, 11.7, and 18.3 μm. These wavelengths are particularly useful for detecting thermal emission from warm dust surrounding deeply embedded protostars and for distinguishing individual sources within the dense cloud core.

The observations confirmed CB54YC1-II as a protostellar source. Its mid-infrared emission is consistent with a protostar of approximately 0.8 M☉ and a mid-infrared luminosity of about 8 L☉. This detection supports the interpretation that CB54YC1-II is an actively forming, low-mass star surrounded by heated circumstellar material.

In contrast, CB54YC1-I was not detected at any of the observed wavelengths. The non-detection does not necessarily mean that the source is absent. It may be hidden behind a very large amount of dust, which would strongly absorb its mid-infrared radiation, or it may possess a circumstellar disk viewed nearly edge-on. Such a geometry could obscure the central protostar even at mid-infrared wavelengths.

The imaging also revealed three compact sources with characteristic temperatures of roughly 100 K in the dense core of CB54. Their cool temperatures and embedded locations suggest that they may be Class 0 protostars—objects in an extremely early evolutionary phase whose radiation is dominated by emission from their surrounding envelopes. If this interpretation is correct, CB54 contains several young stellar objects at different stages of formation. The results therefore indicate that star formation in the globule is more complex than can be inferred from the previously suspected sources alone and identify the dense core as an important target for further high-resolution infrared and submillimeter observations.
outputs.L5:
## Bok: A Word with Many Meanings

“Bok” is a short word with surprisingly diverse meanings. In Afrikaans and Dutch, it can refer to a goat or antelope and appears in the name “Springbok,” South Africa’s famous national animal and rugby symbol. In Korean culture, *bok* is associated with good fortune, happiness, and blessings. Bok is also used as a surname in several countries.

Because of these varied associations, the meaning of Bok depends heavily on language and context. Whether it represents wildlife, sporting pride, family heritage, or prosperity, the word carries cultural significance across different parts of the world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract summarizing mid-infrared observations of protostellar sources in the Bok globule CB54, including wavelengths, luminosity and mass estimates, non-detections, and newly discovered Class 0 candidates.
counterfactuals.output: We present diffraction-limited 11.7 and 18.3 μm imaging of the embedded protostellar population in the Bok globule CB54. The IRAS source is resolved into several compact mid-infrared objects. The brightest source is detected in both bands and has an estimated luminosity of order \(10^{2}\,L_{\odot}\), consistent with an intermediate-mass protostar of roughly \(3\!-\!5\,M_{\odot}\). Fainter sources have luminosities of only a few to a few tens of \(L_{\odot}\) and are associated with compact millimetre cores containing approximately \(1\!-\!10\,M_{\odot}\) of circumstellar material. Several previously identified near-infrared or millimetre sources remain undetected at 11.7 μm, and some are visible only at 18.3 μm, demonstrating the high and spatially variable extinction toward the cluster. Two newly identified mid-infrared sources lack near-infrared counterparts, possess very red spectral-energy distributions, and coincide with dense dust condensations; these characteristics make them strong new Class 0 protostellar candidates. The observations show that CB54 contains a compact, heterogeneous group of young stellar objects spanning the Class 0 and Class I evolutionary phases.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the key findings of a study using 10.4, 11.7, and 18.3 micron imaging to identify and characterize young stellar objects in CB54.
counterfactuals.output:
Mid-infrared imaging of the Bok globule CB54 at 10.4, 11.7, and 18.3 µm showed that the IRAS source is not a single object but a compact group of young stellar objects.

Key findings were:

- The observations resolved the central emission into several distinct mid-IR sources, commonly labeled MIR-a, MIR-b, and MIR-c, demonstrating ongoing clustered or multiple star formation.
- The sources have very red spectral energy distributions and strong circumstellar-envelope emission, identifying them as embedded, early-stage YSOs—primarily Class I or possibly even younger objects.
- Some mid-IR sources correspond to previously known near-IR objects, while at least one is much more deeply obscured and weak or absent at shorter wavelengths.
- Differences between the 10–12 µm and 18.3 µm emission indicate varying dust temperatures and extinctions; silicate absorption near 10 µm likely suppresses the shortest-wavelength flux.
- The mid-IR positions, together with associations with molecular-gas peaks, maser/radio emission, and outflow structures, helped identify the most embedded sources as likely contributors to—though not always uniquely the drivers of—the energetic outflow activity in CB54.
- Overall, the study concluded that CB54 contains a small, young stellar group rather than one dominant protostar, with members at different evolutionary stages embedded in the same dense core.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise astronomy paper abstract about mid-IR detections in CB54, focusing on CB54YC1-II, possible explanations for the non-detection of CB54YC1-I, and three new sources associated with the dense core.
counterfactuals.output: We present mid-infrared observations of the Bok globule CB54 that detect emission from the young stellar object CB54YC1-II and reveal three previously unreported sources projected toward the dense core. The detection of CB54YC1-II confirms the presence of warm circumstellar material and supports its classification as an embedded protostar. In contrast, CB54YC1-I remains undetected at mid-IR wavelengths. This non-detection may result from greater line-of-sight extinction, a colder and more deeply embedded evolutionary state, source variability, or positional/source-confusion uncertainties in earlier identifications. The three new mid-IR sources are spatially associated with the high-column-density core and are therefore candidate embedded young stellar objects, although contamination by unrelated background objects cannot be excluded. These results indicate that star formation in CB54 is more complex than previously recognized and motivate higher-resolution, multiwavelength observations to establish the nature and evolutionary status of the core population.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: What did mid-infrared imaging reveal about the suspected protostellar components CB54YC1-I and CB54YC1-II in the Bok globule CB54?
counterfactuals.output: Mid-infrared images showed that **CB54YC1-I contains compact—apparently multiple—mid-IR emission associated with an embedded young star**, whereas **CB54YC1-II has no corresponding compact mid-IR source**. Thus YC1-II is more likely a knot of scattered or shock-excited emission, rather than a second protostar; the proposed YC1-I/YC1-II protostellar binary was not confirmed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a technical research summary reporting the estimated mid-infrared luminosity and central mass of CB54YC1-II, interpretations of CB54YC1-I, and evidence that three newly detected ∼100 K objects may be embedded Class 0 protostars.
counterfactuals.output:
- **CB54YC1‑II:** Its integrated mid-infrared output is estimated to be of order **\(8\,L_\odot\)**. Comparison with protostellar/accretion models implies a central object of roughly **\(0.5\,M_\odot\)**, although both values are model- and extinction-dependent.

- **CB54YC1‑I:** Its extended near-infrared appearance need not represent a separate, directly visible star. It can be interpreted as **scattered light from an embedded source escaping through an outflow cavity**, with some emission possibly arising from **shock-excited material in the flow**. Thus YC1‑I may be a reflection/outflow feature rather than an independent point-like YSO; an embedded stellar interpretation cannot be completely excluded.

- **Three newly detected \(\sim100\) K sources:** Their very red mid-infrared colors imply dust color temperatures near **100 K**. They lack convincing optical or near-infrared counterparts, lie within the dense millimeter/submillimeter core, and are associated spatially with other signs of active star formation—compact dust emission and, in some cases, molecular-outflow or maser activity. Their cold SEDs, heavy obscuration, and location in dense envelopes therefore make them strong **embedded Class 0 protostar candidates**, rather than ordinary reddened field stars or more evolved Class I/II objects.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
